entries.title: How can a program find something in a sorted list?
entries.answer: Think of looking for the number 82 in a long row of cards already in order. You can look at the card in the middle. If it is 50, you can skip all the lower cards because 82 must be farther right. Look at the new middle of that remaining part and make the same decision. In a binary search, each step narrows the choices to about half of what came before. You cannot do that safely if the cards are scrambled.
facts: Binary search needs a way to tell which side of the current place the wanted item could be on.

entries.title: How can a program make a choice?
entries.answer: A program can follow different instructions depending on what has happened. A game can ask whether the player has reached the end of a path. If the answer is yes, it can show a sign that says the round is over. If the answer is no, it can keep the path open. The check is called a condition. This lets one program handle more than one situation without needing a separate set of instructions for every possible round.
facts: A condition has a result the program can treat as true or false.

entries.title: How can a program put a list in order?
entries.answer: To order a pile of numbered cards, you could make a short row and slide each new card into its place. If the row says 2, 4, and 8, a new card with 5 goes after 4. A program can follow a similar method. It compares one value with nearby values and keeps the ordered part of its list in order as it grows. Other ways may use fewer comparisons on some lists. The kind of work matters when the list is large.
facts: Some sorting methods move one item at a time into an already ordered section.

entries.title: How can you predict the next part of a pattern?
entries.answer: Read these colors aloud: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. The smallest block that keeps repeating is red, blue, blue. If that rule continues, the next color is red. Seeing only a few colors does not always tell you the rule for sure. Another person might be following a different rule that begins the same way. Looking for a repeating block gives you a guess you can check against more of the pattern.
facts: A pattern can repeat sounds, moves, shapes, or numbers.

entries.title: How does a number machine work?
entries.answer: A number machine is a way to picture a rule. Put in a number, follow the same rule each time, and see what number comes out. If the rule is to add three, an input of two gives an output of five, and an input of four gives seven. A two-step rule could first double the input and then add one. In that rule the order matters.
facts: The rule add three gives an output of three when the input is zero.

entries.title: How does Boolean logic use true and false?
entries.answer: Some computer questions have two possible answers. A door is open or it is not. A player has a key or does not. Boolean logic lets a program work with true and false answers like these. It can put several answers together to make a longer test. The programmer needs to know exactly what each check means. Even a big choice can often be broken into small questions that a program can answer clearly.
facts: Boolean values can be represented with bits.

entries.title: What can a truth table show you?
entries.answer: A truth table is a chart for checking a logic rule. Suppose a sign responds to two buttons. You can make one row for neither button pushed, one for only the first, one for only the second, and one for both. Then write what the sign does in every row. A table helps reveal an answer you might have missed. Programmers and engineers can use it to compare rules before they write a program or build a circuit.
facts: A table for two true-or-false inputs has four rows if it lists every possibility.

entries.title: What does NOT do to a logic value?
entries.answer: If a light is on, the sentence “the light is not on” is false. If the light is off, that sentence is true. The logic rule NOT flips a true-or-false answer. It is useful when a program needs to check the opposite of a question it can already ask. A game that knows whether its menu is open might also want to know whether the menu is not open, so it can let a player move.
facts: Applying NOT twice to a true-or-false value gives you back the starting value.

entries.title: What rule means one or the other, but never both?
entries.answer: An imaginary sign might light up when only one person presses a button. If neither presses a button, it stays dark. If both press at once, it also stays dark. That rule is called XOR, or exclusive OR. It has only two ways to get a true answer with two buttons. Exactly one of the two buttons must be pressed. This is different from the usual OR rule, where pressing both would also turn the sign on.
facts: XOR is short for exclusive OR.

entries.title: When does an AND rule say yes?
entries.answer: Imagine a pretend treasure chest that opens only when you have a key and stand on a marked square. You need both parts. Having just the key does not open it, and standing on the square alone does not open it either. A computer can combine the two checks using an AND rule. It gets a true result when both checks are true together. That result can then tell the game to open the chest.
facts: The AND result is false if either of its two checks is false.

entries.title: When does an OR rule say yes?
entries.answer: Suppose a pretend gate opens if you have a round token or a square token. With either token the gate opens. If you have both, it can open too. This is the usual OR rule in computing. A true result means at least one part of the test is true. People sometimes say “or” when they mean you must choose just one thing. In logic, there is a different rule for allowing exactly one.
facts: For the ordinary logic OR rule, both inputs being true also gives a true result.

entries.title: Why do programs use loops?
entries.answer: A loop tells a program to go through the same group of steps more than once. An animation might use a loop to move a picture a little, show it, and move it again. One loop could run ten times. Another could keep going until the picture reaches the edge. Deciding when to stop is part of writing the loop. If the stopping test never happens, a program may keep doing the same job again and again.
facts: A loop can repeat a fixed number of times or while a test is true.
